overview.intro:
Chapter 81 covers the base metals that are not iron, copper, nickel, aluminum, lead, zinc or tin: **tungsten** (8101), **molybdenum** (8102), **tantalum** (8103), **magnesium** (8104), **cobalt** (8105), **bismuth** (8106), **titanium** (8108), **zirconium** (8109), **antimony** (8110), **manganese** (8111), the minor metals of 8112 (beryllium, chromium, hafnium, rhenium, thallium, cadmium, gallium, germanium, indium, niobium, vanadium) and **cermets** (8113). Several, such as gallium, germanium, indium and cobalt, are named as critical minerals in Proclamation 11001. Base rates run from **Free to 15%** (unwrought titanium and titanium mill products); 24 of the 84 lines are Free. Molybdenum powder and unwrought molybdenum, and other magnesium articles, carry a compound rate charged per kilogram of metal content plus a percentage.

**No Section 232 tariff applies.** Proclamation 11001 (January 14, 2026) found that imports of processed critical minerals threaten national security but chose negotiations, not tariffs. The duties that do apply come from Section 301. The **2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies** (10% or 12.5%) exempt 52 of the 84 lines through the note 52(b) list (tungsten powder and scrap, tantalum, magnesium, cobalt, bismuth, titanium, antimony, unwrought manganese, chromium, rhenium, gallium, germanium, indium, niobium); unwrought and wrought tungsten, molybdenum, zirconium, manganese scrap and articles, beryllium, hafnium, unwrought thallium, cadmium, unwrought vanadium and cermets pay it. **China** pays 25% under Section 301 on 59 lines (List 3, and note 31 for tungsten, tantalum, chromium and indium). Canadian **cermets** pay a 50% Section 338 duty, even with a USMCA claim. Russian goods pay column 2 rates, or 70% on titanium sponge and some minor metals.

**Antidumping duty orders** cover pure, granular and alloy magnesium from China and tungsten shot from China. They are company-specific and not part of this table or the tariff calculator.

stats.label: Lines with an extra duty for some origins
stats.note: 2026 Section 301 (60 economies): 32 lines (the other 52 are on the note 52(b) exemption list); Brazil Section 301: 32; China Section 301 at 25% (List 3, note 31): 59; Canada Section 338: 1 (cermets); Russia 70% in lieu of column 2: 11. USMCA goods are exempt from the Section 301 duties but not from Section 338.

productGroups.label: Tungsten (wolfram) and articles
productGroups.blurb: Tungsten powder, unwrought tungsten and sintered bars, wire, waste and scrap, and wrought tungsten (bars, rods, plates, sheet, foil) and other articles: 6 lines, 2.8% to 7%. Powder and scrap are on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list; unwrought tungsten, wire and other articles pay it. Chinese tungsten pays 25% under Section 301 (note 31) on top.

productGroups.label: Molybdenum and articles
productGroups.blurb: Molybdenum powder and unwrought molybdenum (charged per kg of molybdenum content plus a percentage), bars and rods, wire, scrap and other articles: 7 lines, Free to 6.6%. None is on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list, so every molybdenum line pays it.
productGroups.rateSummary: 9.1¢/kg on molybdenum content + 1.2% · 13.9¢/kg on molybdenum content + 1.9% · 6.6% · 4.4% · Free · 3.7%

productGroups.label: Tantalum and articles
productGroups.blurb: Unwrought tantalum and powder, waste and scrap, crucibles and other tantalum articles: 5 lines, Free to 4.4%. All on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list; Chinese unwrought tantalum and powder pay 25% (note 31).

productGroups.label: Magnesium and articles
productGroups.blurb: Unwrought magnesium (pure, at least 99.8%, and alloy), waste and scrap, raspings, turnings, granules and powder, and other magnesium articles: 5 lines, Free to 8% (other articles 14.8¢/kg on magnesium content + 3.5%). All on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list. Chinese pure, granular and alloy magnesium is under antidumping orders.

productGroups.label: Cobalt mattes, cobalt and articles
productGroups.blurb: Cobalt mattes and other intermediate products, unwrought cobalt (alloys and other), powders, waste and scrap and other cobalt articles: 5 lines, Free to 4.4%. All on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list; Chinese cobalt pays 25% (List 3).

productGroups.label: Bismuth and articles
productGroups.blurb: Bismuth over 99.99% pure and other bismuth and articles, including waste and scrap: 2 lines, both Free. On the 2026 Section 301 exemption list; Chinese bismuth pays 25% (List 3).

productGroups.label: Titanium and articles
productGroups.blurb: Titanium sponge, powder, ingots and other unwrought titanium (15%), scrap (Free), titanium castings and articles (5.5%) and mill products (blooms, slabs, bars, wire, plate, sheet, foil, tubes, 15%): 12 lines. All on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list. Chinese titanium pays 25% (List 3); Russian unwrought titanium and scrap 70%.

productGroups.label: Zirconium and articles
productGroups.blurb: Unwrought zirconium and powders, waste and scrap, and other zirconium articles, each split by hafnium content (nuclear-grade, under 1 part hafnium to 500 parts zirconium, or other): 6 lines, Free to 4.2%. None is on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list.

productGroups.label: Antimony and articles
productGroups.blurb: Unwrought antimony and powders, waste and scrap, and other antimony articles: 3 lines, all Free. On the 2026 Section 301 exemption list and on no China list, so antimony is Free from every country except column 2 countries.

productGroups.label: Manganese and articles
productGroups.blurb: Manganese waste and scrap (Free), unwrought manganese flake and powder of at least 99.5% and other unwrought manganese (14%), and other manganese articles (3.7%): 5 lines. Unwrought manganese is on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list; scrap and articles are not.

productGroups.label: Beryllium, chromium, hafnium, rhenium, thallium, cadmium, gallium, germanium, indium, niobium, vanadium
productGroups.blurb: Beryllium, chromium, hafnium, rhenium, thallium and cadmium (unwrought, scrap, other), and the 8112.92 / 8112.99 lines for gallium, germanium, indium, niobium and vanadium: 27 lines, Free to 8.5%. Chromium, rhenium, gallium, germanium, indium, niobium and wrought vanadium are on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list; beryllium, hafnium, cadmium, unwrought thallium, unwrought vanadium and 8112.92 waste and scrap are not.

productGroups.label: Cermets and articles
productGroups.blurb: Cermets (sintered metal and ceramic composites, such as cemented tungsten carbide that is not a tool tip) and articles of cermets, including waste and scrap: 1 line, 3.7%. Pays the 2026 Section 301 duty; Canadian cermets pay the 50% Section 338 duty since August 22, 2026.

spiLegend.name: Agreement on Trade in Civil Aircraft

workedExamples.title: $1 million of titanium sponge from Japan
workedExamples.body: Titanium sponge has a **15%** general rate, the highest in the chapter. Japan has no FTA with the United States, and unwrought titanium is on the note 52(b) list, so Japan's 2026 Section 301 duty (12.5% floor, 9903.05.49) does not apply. Total: **15%, or $150,000**. The same sponge from Kazakhstan also pays 15%; from China, 15% + 25% (List 3, 9903.88.03) = 40%; from Russia, 70% in place of the column 2 rate (9903.90.09).

workedExamples.title: Titanium tubes with attached fittings for civil aircraft, from the United Kingdom
workedExamples.body: Titanium tubes and pipes carry **15%**. The "Free (C)" special rate applies, under additional U.S. note 2 to Chapter 81, only to tubes and pipes **with attached fittings, suitable for conducting gases or liquids**, that are certified for use in civil aircraft (general note 6, 19 CFR 10.183). With that certification the duty is **Free**; plain titanium sheet or bar for an aircraft does not qualify. Titanium mill products are exempt from the UK's 10% Section 301 duty (note 52(b)).

workedExamples.title: Tungsten powder vs unwrought tungsten from China
workedExamples.body: Tungsten powder carries **7%** plus **25%** Section 301 (note 31(b), 9903.91.01, since September 27, 2024) = **32%**; it is on the note 52(b) list, so the 12.5% 2026 duty on China does not apply. Unwrought tungsten and sintered bars (8101.94) pay **6.6% + 25%** (note 31(j), 9903.91.11, since January 1, 2025) **+ 12.5%** (9903.05.31) = **44.1%**. On $100,000 that is $32,000 for powder and $44,100 for unwrought metal. Tungsten shot (often entered under 8101.99.80) from China also carries antidumping and countervailing duty orders.

workedExamples.title: Molybdenum powder from the United Kingdom: a duty on metal content
workedExamples.body: The rate is **9.1¢/kg on molybdenum content + 1.2%**. The importer must declare the net weight of molybdenum contained, not just the gross weight. For 2,000 kg of powder containing 1,998 kg of molybdenum, worth $120,000: 1,998 × $0.091 = $181.82, plus 1.2% of $120,000 = $1,440. Molybdenum is not on the note 52(b) list, so the UK's 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.81) adds $12,000: **$13,621.82 in total (about 11.4%)**. From the EU the 2026 duty is 10% in place of the base rate when that is lower, so the same shipment pays $12,000 (10%).

workedExamples.title: Pure magnesium ingot from China
workedExamples.body: Unwrought magnesium of at least 99.8% carries **8%**. It is on the note 52(b) list and on no China Section 301 list, so the tariff is just **8%**. But pure magnesium from China has been under an **antidumping duty order since 1995**: Commerce's last sunset review found margins of up to 108.26% likely to prevail, and each exporter pays its own cash-deposit rate. Alloy magnesium (8104.19) and granular magnesium (8104.30) from China are under separate orders.

workedExamples.title: Cermets from Canada, with a USMCA certification
workedExamples.body: Cermets carry **3.7%**, which USMCA reduces to Free, and USMCA goods are exempt from Canada's 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.93). But cermets are on the Section 338 list (note 51(b)(3), 9903.03.14), which charges **50%** even when USMCA is claimed: **50%** with USMCA, **63.7%** without (3.7% + 10% + 50%). In effect since August 22, 2026.

workedExamples.title: Gallium and germanium from China
workedExamples.body: Unwrought gallium carries **3%** plus **25%** under List 3 (9903.88.03) = **28%**; it is on the note 52(b) list, so the 12.5% 2026 duty does not apply. notes.additionalUsNotes:
**1.** Alloys of each of the base metals of Chapter 81 are metals in which the content of that base metal is, by weight, less than 99 percent, but not less than any other metallic element.

**2.** For subheading 8108.90.60, the "Free (C)" special rate (civil aircraft) applies only to tubes and pipes with attached fittings, suitable for conducting gases or liquids.

Statistical units: tungsten powder and scrap are also reported in kilograms of tungsten content (W kg), alloy magnesium and some magnesium products in kilograms of magnesium content (Mg kg), and vanadium in kilograms of vanadium (V kg).

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 81: Other Base Metals; Cermets; Articles Thereof — Tariff Updates

seo.title: Critical Minerals Tariff Updates 2025–2026: Tungsten, Titanium, Magnesium, Section 232 & Section 301 (HTS Ch. 81) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Every U.S. tariff change for HTS Chapter 81 metals with official sources: the Section 232 critical minerals decision (no tariff), China's 25% Section 301 duty on tungsten, the 2026 Section 301 exemption list, Canada's Section 338 duty on cermets, the end of the IEEPA duties and the magnesium and tungsten shot AD/CVD orders.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule, the **2025 Basic Edition** (in force January 1, 2025) and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026), and lists every extra duty that reaches Chapter 81 today. **Base rates did not move**: all 84 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates.

The extra duties changed. The **Section 232 investigation of processed critical minerals** (opened April 2025) ended on January 14, 2026 with Proclamation 11001, which chose negotiations over tariffs, so no Section 232 duty applies. The IEEPA duties ended on **February 24, 2026**; most Chapter 81 lines had been exempt from the reciprocal tariff (Annex II) and from the Section 122 surcharge that followed. Since **July 24, 2026** the **2026 Section 301 tariffs** charge 10% or 12.5% on 32 lines from 60 economies; the other 52 lines are on the note 52(b) exemption list. **China** pays 25% under Section 301 on 59 lines (raised for tungsten, tantalum, chromium and indium in 2024–2025), **Brazil** 25% more on the same 32 lines, and **Canadian cermets** 50% under Section 338 since August 22, 2026.

Antidumping orders on Chinese magnesium and tungsten shot are listed for reference; they are company-specific and **not included in the tariff calculator**.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 81 from any country: China Section 301 (notes 20 and 31), the 2026 Section 301 actions on 60 economies and Brazil (notes 50, 52), Canada Section 338 (note 51), Russia's rates in lieu of column 2 (note 30), the scheduled Nicaragua Section 301 duty (note 29), and the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties. No Section 232 heading reaches Chapter 81 (the opt-in Section 232 certified-parts elections for vehicle parts are left off this page). The Section 232 critical minerals decision and the magnesium and tungsten shot AD/CVD orders are listed for reference. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 81 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 84 Chapter 81 tariff lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; no line was added, removed or renumbered.

changes.title: China Section 301 duties continue during the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR received requests to continue the 2018 China actions, so they did not terminate on their anniversaries and remain in effect pending the statutory review. The 25% List 3 and note 31 duties on Chinese Chapter 81 metals continue.

changes.title: Five-year review of the alloy magnesium order on China begins
changes.detail: Commerce and the ITC began the fourth five-year (sunset) review of the 2005 antidumping duty order on alloy magnesium (magnesium metal) from China (A-570-896, 731-TA-1071). Responses to the ITC were due November 2, 2026. The order stays in force during the review.

changes.title: Pure magnesium from China: margin amended after a court ruling
changes.detail: After the Court of International Trade sustained Commerce's remand on the electricity surrogate value (Tianjin Magnesium International v. United States, final judgment August 14, 2026), Commerce amended the 2022–2023 review result for Tianjin Magnesium International / Tianjin Magnesium Metal (previously 25.26%) and will issue revised cash-deposit instructions to CBP.

changes.title: Section 338 duty on Canadian cermets
changes.detail: Proclamation 11048 put a 50% Section 338 duty (9903.03.14, note 51(b)(3)) on a list of Canadian products that includes cermets (8113.00.00); Proclamation 11056 moved the start from August 19 to August 22, 2026. The duty applies even to USMCA goods. Proclamation 11065 later changed the list from September 15, 2026 (adding aluminum extrusions and tubes) but left cermets on it. No other Chapter 81 line is covered.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies: 52 of 84 lines exempt
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% duties on goods of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect. The note 52(b) list (9903.05.86) exempts 52 Chapter 81 lines: tungsten powder and scrap, tantalum, magnesium, cobalt, bismuth, titanium, antimony, unwrought manganese, chromium, rhenium, gallium, germanium, indium, niobium and vanadium (8112.99.20). The other 32 pay: unwrought and wrought tungsten, molybdenum, zirconium, manganese scrap and articles, beryllium, hafnium, unwrought thallium, cadmium, unwrought vanadium and cermets. The EU, Japan, Korea and Taiwan pay 10% or 12.5% in place of a lower base rate; USMCA goods are exempt.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026. Its exemption list (9903.03.03) covered the same Chapter 81 metals as the later note 52(b) list, except vanadium (8112.99.20).

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Brazil: 25%, critical metals exempt
changes.detail: The 25% duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect. Its exemption list (note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03) has the same Chapter 81 lines as note 52(b), so Brazilian niobium, chromium, titanium and other listed metals are exempt; molybdenum, zirconium, beryllium and cermets pay 25% plus the 12.5% 2026 duty.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply.

changes.title: AGOA duty-free treatment extended through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: Proclamation 11030 implemented the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026: AGOA (SPI D) applies through December 31, 2026. Madagascar and South Africa, which ship cobalt and manganese, are listed beneficiaries (general note 16). Most Chapter 81 lines carry SPI D; unwrought manganese other than flake (8111.00.49) does not.

changes.title: USTR consults on a plurilateral critical-minerals agreement
changes.detail: Following Proclamation 11001, USTR requested comments on the design of a plurilateral agreement on trade in critical minerals and on policy actions such as price floors. No tariff has been set on Chapter 81 metals.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs; most Chapter 81 metals exempt
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. 41 Chapter 81 subheadings were on its exemption list (9903.03.03), as were USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico. Molybdenum, zirconium, beryllium, hafnium, cadmium, unwrought thallium and vanadium, cermets and tungsten other than powder and scrap paid it.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Section 232 processed critical minerals: negotiations, no tariff
changes.detail: Proclamation 11001 concurred with Commerce's finding (report of October 24, 2025) that imports of processed critical minerals and their derivative products threaten national security, but directed Commerce and USTR to negotiate agreements, considering price floors, instead of imposing tariffs, with an update due within 180 days; minimum import prices were named as a possible later remedy. No Section 232 duty applies to Chapter 81.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29). Note 29 has no critical-minerals exemption, so it will reach all 84 lines. The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: China IEEPA duties cut; China commits to ease critical-mineral export controls
changes.detail: Executive Order 14357 cut the China fentanyl duty from 20% to 10% and Executive Order 14358 kept the reciprocal duty on China at 10%, both from November 10, 2025, under the Kuala Lumpur arrangement. In it China committed to postpone and effectively eliminate its current and proposed export controls on rare earth elements and other critical minerals. Those controls are Chinese export rules, not U.S. import duties. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: AD/CVD orders on tungsten shot from China
changes.detail: Commerce issued antidumping and countervailing duty orders on tungsten shot (spheres 1.5 to 10 mm, at least 92.6% tungsten) from China, entered under 9306.29.00 or 8101.99.80. The China-wide antidumping rate is 201.32% and the all-others subsidy rate 55.64%; the ITC found material retardation of the U.S. industry.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods from 25% to 35% (9903.01.10); energy and critical minerals as defined by 30 U.S.C. 1606(a)(3) (9903.01.13) stayed at 10%. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14298 cut the reciprocal duty on China from 125% to 10% for 90 days, later extended. The Annex II exemption still covered most Chapter 81 lines; the 20% fentanyl duty applied to all of them. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Section 232 investigation of processed critical minerals opened
changes.detail: Executive Order 14272 told Commerce to investigate imports of processed critical minerals and their derivative products under Section 232; BIS asked for public comments on April 25, 2025. It ended with Proclamation 11001 (no tariff).

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff: most Chapter 81 metals exempt
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and country rates (9903.02.xx) on products of all countries except Canada and Mexico, from April 5, 2025. 41 Chapter 81 subheadings were on the Annex II exemption list (U.S. note 2(v)(iii)): tungsten powder and scrap, tantalum, magnesium, cobalt, bismuth, titanium, antimony, unwrought manganese, chromium, rhenium, gallium, germanium, indium, niobium and other 8112 metals. Molybdenum, zirconium, beryllium, hafnium, cadmium, unwrought thallium and vanadium, manganese scrap and articles, cermets and unwrought and wrought tungsten (other than powder and scrap) paid. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: USMCA goods exempted from the Canada and Mexico duties
changes.detail: From March 7, 2025, goods entered under USMCA were exempt from the IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty raised to 20%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14228 added another 10% (9903.01.24) to the IEEPA duty on products of China (9903.01.20), for 20% in total. No Chapter 81 line was exempt. Cut to 10% on November 10, 2025; ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: IEEPA duties on Canada, Mexico and China
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01) from March 4, 2025, with 10% for Canadian energy and critical minerals (9903.01.13), and +10% on goods of China (9903.01.20) from February 4, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China: 25% on tungsten products
changes.detail: After its four-year review USTR raised the Section 301 duty on Chinese unwrought tungsten, sintered bars and wrought tungsten (8101.94, 8101.99.10, 8101.99.80; note 31(j), 9903.91.11) to 25%, together with wafers and polysilicon.

changes.title: China: 25% on critical minerals (four-year review)
changes.detail: USTR's four-year review added a 25% duty (note 31(b), 9903.91.01) on Chinese tungsten powder (8101.10), unwrought tantalum and powder (8103.20), unwrought chromium (8112.21) and indium (8112.92.30), among other critical minerals.

changes.title: Granular pure magnesium order on China continued
changes.detail: After a fourth five-year review, Commerce continued the 2001 antidumping duty order on pure magnesium in granular form (raspings, granules, turnings, chips, powder) from China; it had found margins of up to 305.56% likely to prevail.

changes.title: Pure magnesium order on China continued
changes.detail: After a fifth five-year review, Commerce continued the 1995 antidumping duty order on pure magnesium (ingot) from China, which covers 8104.11, 8104.19 and other subheadings; it had found margins of up to 108.26% likely to prevail.

changes.title: Russia: 70% on titanium and minor metals
changes.detail: Proclamation 10523 set a 70% rate in place of column 2 (9903.90.09, note 30(d)) on Russian unwrought titanium and powders, titanium scrap, hafnium, rhenium scrap, gallium, indium, niobium and 8112.92 waste and scrap.

changes.title: Russia moved to column 2 rates
changes.detail: The Suspending Normal Trade Relations with Russia and Belarus Act applied column 2 rates to products of Russia and Belarus from April 9, 2022. In Chapter 81 these run from Free to 100% (pure magnesium).

changes.title: Alloy magnesium (magnesium metal) order on China continued
changes.detail: After a third five-year review, Commerce continued the 2005 antidumping duty order on magnesium metal (alloy magnesium) from China; it had found margins of up to 141.49% likely to prevail.

changes.title: Section 232 titanium sponge: no tariff, a working group instead
changes.detail: Commerce found (report of November 29, 2019) that titanium sponge imports threaten to impair national security. On February 27, 2020 the President directed an interagency Titanium Sponge Working Group, not tariffs, to ensure access to sponge for defense; its report was posted in July 2023. No Section 232 duty was imposed on titanium sponge.

changes.title: No AD/CVD orders on magnesium from Israel
changes.detail: Commerce had found dumping and subsidies on magnesium from Israel (8104.11, 8104.19, 8104.30), but the ITC determined that the U.S. industry was not materially injured or threatened, so no orders were issued.

changes.title: China List 3 raised to 25%
changes.detail: List 3 (9903.88.03) took effect at 10% on September 24, 2018 and rose to 25% on May 10, 2019. In Chapter 81 it covers cobalt, bismuth, titanium, magnesium powder and articles, zirconium scrap and articles, tungsten and molybdenum wire, most 8112 metals and cermets.

changes.title: No AD/CVD case on titanium sponge from Japan and Kazakhstan
changes.detail: The ITC found no reasonable indication of injury from titanium sponge (8108.20.00) from Japan and Kazakhstan, ending the antidumping and countervailing duty investigations at the preliminary stage.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 81 metals and cermets were **$3.92B in 2025**, +5.6% from $3.71B in 2024 and up from $2.24B in 2020. The five largest suppliers were Japan ($567M), China ($475M), Germany ($411M), United Kingdom ($313M), Canada ($296M). By product group the largest were titanium (8108, $1.19B), minor metals (8112, $649M), cobalt (8105, $486M): titanium alone, mostly sponge and mill products, was about 30% of the total, and Japan shipped $567M, mostly titanium.

Imports from **China fell 36%**, from $746M in 2024 to $475M in 2025. In 2025 Chinese goods also paid the IEEPA duties (the fentanyl duty on every line, the reciprocal duty on lines outside Annex II), and Chinese unwrought and wrought tungsten a new 25% Section 301 rate from January 1, 2025. Among the fastest-growing suppliers were Thailand ($47M to $129M, mainly antimony), Kazakhstan ($83M to $109M, mainly titanium). Canada shipped $296M, led by cobalt ($89M); USMCA-qualifying Canadian metal is Free.

2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

seo.shortDescription: The total U.S. tariff on tungsten, titanium, magnesium, cobalt, molybdenum and other Chapter 81 metals from each major supplier: base rate plus the 2026 Section 301 duty on 32 lines, China's 25%, Brazil 37.5%, Canadian cermets 50%, Russia's column 2 and 70% rates, and the FTA and USMCA preferences.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duties for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. Three things decide the total: whether the line is on the **note 52(b) exemption list** (then no 2026 Section 301 duty applies: titanium, tantalum, magnesium, cobalt, bismuth, antimony, unwrought manganese, chromium, gallium, germanium, indium, niobium, tungsten powder and scrap), whether the supplier is **China** (25% Section 301 on 59 lines), and whether a **free trade agreement** removes the base rate.

So Japanese titanium sponge pays its 15% base rate, Chinese sponge 40%, Kazakh sponge 15% and Russian sponge 70%; molybdenum, zirconium and cermets pay their base rate plus 10% or 12.5% from most suppliers, and Canadian cermets pay 50% under Section 338 even with USMCA. The table does **not** include the antidumping duties on Chinese magnesium and tungsten shot.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 81: Other Base Metals; Cermets; Articles Thereof — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Tungsten, Titanium & Other Chapter 81 Metals: Entry Rules & Ways to Lower Duty | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The rules for each HTS Chapter 81 line (TSCA certification, marking, Section 301 and Section 338 entry, magnesium and tungsten shot AD/CVD scope) and the legal ways to pay less: the note 52(b) exemption list, USMCA and FTA claims, AGOA, civil aircraft titanium tubes, metal processed abroad (9802.00.60), origin and drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
For Chapter 81, the duty mostly depends on **which line the metal falls in and where it comes from**. The 2026 Section 301 exemption list (note 52(b)) works line by line: tungsten powder is exempt but unwrought tungsten is not; unwrought germanium and manganese are exempt, wrought molybdenum and cermets are not. China's Section 301 duty adds 25% on most lines, and Canada's Section 338 duty adds 50% to cermets.

The legal ways to pay less: classify correctly (powder, unwrought, scrap and wrought metal are separate lines), claim **USMCA**, an **FTA** or **AGOA**, use the **civil aircraft** rate for titanium tubes with fittings, enter metal processed abroad from U.S. material under **9802.00.60**, avoid Chinese origin on listed lines, check **AD/CVD scope** for magnesium and tungsten shot, and claim **drawback** on re-exports. Each rule and lever links to its regulation.

levers.title: Classify the form of the metal correctly (note 52(b) list)
levers.saves: The 10% or 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (and Brazil's 25%) on lines on the note 52(b) exemption list
levers.appliesTo: All 84 lines; the exempt and non-exempt lines sit side by side in 8101, 8111 and 8112
levers.document: Technical specifications (form, purity, whether sintered, worked or alloyed) and, if unsure, a CBP binding ruling. Report 9903.05.86 with the exempt line.
levers.caveat: Classification follows the product, not the duty: tungsten powder (8101.10) is exempt, unwrought tungsten and sintered bars (8101.94) are not; unwrought germanium (8112.92.60) is exempt, other germanium (8112.99.10) too, but unwrought vanadium (8112.92.70) is not. Molybdenum, zirconium and cermets have no exempt line.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(b), heading 9903.05.86

levers.title: Claim USMCA for Canadian and Mexican metal
levers.saves: The base rate (up to 15% on titanium, 14% on manganese) and the 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94)
levers.appliesTo: Originating goods of Canada or Mexico on every line
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer (no set format), in the importer's possession when the claim is made; origin under the Chapter 81 tariff-shift rules (waste and scrap originate where collected).
levers.caveat: Does not remove the 50% Section 338 duty on Canadian cermets (8113). The USMCA joint review did not renew the agreement, but it remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(g)–(h)

levers.title: Claim an FTA or AGOA rate
levers.saves: The base rate: Free instead of up to 15% (titanium), 8.5% (beryllium) or 14% (manganese)
levers.appliesTo: Originating goods of Korea, Israel, Chile, Australia and other FTA partners, and of AGOA beneficiaries such as Madagascar and South Africa (SPI D, through December 31, 2026)
levers.document: The origin documentation each agreement requires, and the SPI on the entry line (KR, IL, CL, AU, D and others).
levers.caveat: The 2026 Section 301 duty still applies to the 32 non-exempt lines (for Korea a 12.5% total replaces the base rate). GSP (A, A+, A*) has lapsed and gives no reduction. 8111.00.49 has no AGOA rate.

levers.title: Civil aircraft titanium tubes with attached fittings
levers.saves: The 15% base rate on titanium tubes and pipes (Free under SPI C)
levers.appliesTo: Titanium tubes and pipes with attached fittings, suitable for conducting gases or liquids, of 8108.90.60, for civil aircraft
levers.document: Civil aircraft certification under general note 6 and 19 CFR 10.183 (written certification that the article is for a civil aircraft and FAA-approved where required).
levers.caveat: Additional U.S. note 2 to Chapter 81 limits the Free (C) rate to tubes and pipes with attached fittings: titanium sheet, bar or plain tube for aircraft pays 15%. No 2026 Section 301 duty applies to titanium anyway.

levers.title: U.S. metal processed abroad (9802.00.60)
levers.saves: Duty on the full value: the base rate and the Section 301, Section 338 and Russia duties apply only to the value of the processing abroad
levers.appliesTo: Articles of metal made or processed in the United States, exported for further processing and returned for further processing (for example U.S. titanium or tungsten rolled, drawn or machined abroad)
levers.document: Entry under 9802.00.60 with the declarations of 19 CFR 10.9 (foreign processor and importer) showing the U.S. metal and the cost of processing.
levers.caveat: The returned article must be further processed in the United States. CBP decides whether the claim fits; the Chapter 99 notes (for example 52 and 30) say the extra duties apply to the value of the processing.

provisions.rate: A duty upon the value of such processing outside the United States
provisions.text: Any article of metal manufactured in the United States or subjected to a process of manufacture in the United States, exported for further processing and returned for further processing

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Avoid Chinese origin on listed lines
levers.saves: The 25% Section 301 duty (List 3, note 31) on 59 lines, plus any antidumping duty on magnesium and tungsten shot
levers.appliesTo: All lines on the China lists: tungsten, cobalt, bismuth, titanium, tantalum, most 8112 metals, cermets
levers.document: Mill certificates and production records showing where the metal was smelted, refined or last substantially transformed (origin for Section 301 follows substantial transformation; ask CBP for a binding ruling).
levers.caveat: Remelting or simple processing in a third country may not change origin; Chinese metal that is only repackaged stays Chinese. Antimony, unwrought magnesium and unwrought germanium are on no China list, so origin matters less there (magnesium AD orders still apply).

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20, 31

levers.title: Check AD/CVD scope before you buy
levers.saves: The whole antidumping or countervailing duty, when the product or producer is outside the order
levers.appliesTo: Pure, granular and alloy magnesium from China (8104.11, 8104.19, 8104.30, 8104.90) and tungsten shot from China (8101.99.80, 9306.29)
levers.document: The order's written scope (it, not the HTS number, decides) and the exporter's company-specific cash-deposit rate; when unsure, request a scope ruling from Commerce.
levers.caveat: The three magnesium orders split the product by purity, form and ASTM alloy specification; reagent mixtures with 90% or less magnesium are excluded from the granular and alloy orders. Rates change with each administrative review.

levers.title: Drawback on re-exported metal
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the base rate, Section 301 and other ordinary duties on goods that are exported or used in exported products
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records (19 CFR part 191).
levers.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are never refundable (19 CFR 191.3). Check the Chapter 99 note of each extra duty for drawback limits.

groups.note: Powder and scrap are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; unwrought, wire and wrought tungsten are not. China 25% (note 31). Tungsten shot from China is under AD/CVD orders (8101.99.80).

seo.title: Critical Minerals Tariffs FAQ: Tungsten, Titanium, Magnesium, Cobalt, Gallium & HS Codes (HTS Ch. 81) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about U.S. tariffs on Chapter 81 metals: the Section 232 critical minerals decision, which metals are exempt, tungsten and titanium tariffs, China rates, gallium, germanium and antimony, magnesium antidumping duties, Canadian cermets and the HS codes for titanium, tungsten carbide and cermets.
keywords: is there a tariff on titanium

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most-searched questions about U.S. tariffs on tungsten, titanium, magnesium, cobalt and the other Chapter 81 metals, by country and by HS code. Each answer links to the page with the detail and the official sources.
keyTakeaways: No Section 232 tariff applies to Chapter 81 metals: Proclamation 11001 (January 14, 2026) chose negotiations on processed critical minerals instead of tariffs. Base rates run from Free to 15% (titanium).

The 2026 Section 301 tariffs (10% or 12.5%) exempt 52 of the 84 lines through note 52(b): titanium, tantalum, magnesium, cobalt, bismuth, antimony, chromium, gallium, germanium, indium, niobium, tungsten powder and scrap. Molybdenum, zirconium, beryllium, hafnium, cadmium, unwrought tungsten and cermets pay it.

China pays 25% under Section 301 on 59 lines (44.1% on unwrought tungsten, 40% on titanium sponge); Canadian cermets pay 50% under Section 338 even with USMCA; Russia pays column 2 or 70%. Antidumping orders cover Chinese magnesium and tungsten shot.
In 2025 the U.S. imported $3.92B of Chapter 81 products, Japan ($567M) and China ($475M) first; titanium was the largest group.

faqs.question: Is there a Section 232 tariff on critical minerals?
faqs.answer: No. Commerce investigated imports of processed critical minerals and their derivative products under Section 232 from April 2025 (Executive Order 14272) and reported on October 24, 2025 that they threaten national security. In Proclamation 11001 of January 14, 2026, the President chose to negotiate agreements, considering price floors, instead of imposing tariffs, and said minimum import prices could follow. As of the 2026 Revision 21 schedule, no Section 232 heading covers Chapter 81 metals.

faqs.question: Which critical minerals are exempt from tariffs?
faqs.answer: Under the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, U.S. note 52(b) exempts 52 of the 84 Chapter 81 lines: tungsten powder and scrap, tantalum, magnesium, cobalt, bismuth, titanium, antimony, unwrought manganese, chromium, rhenium, gallium, germanium, indium, niobium and wrought vanadium (heading 9903.05.86). They pay only their base rate (Free to 15%). The exemption does not cover China's 25% Section 301 duty, and molybdenum, zirconium, beryllium, hafnium, cadmium, unwrought tungsten, tungsten wire and cermets are not exempt.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on tungsten?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on tungsten
faqs.answer: Base rates are 2.8% (scrap) to 7% (powder): 6.6% for unwrought tungsten and sintered bars (8101.94), 4.4% for wire, 6.5% for wrought bars, sheet and foil. Powder and scrap are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; unwrought tungsten, wire and other articles pay it (10% or 12.5% more, or 10% / 12.5% in total for the EU, Japan, Korea and Taiwan). FTA partners such as Korea and Israel pay no base rate. Tungsten ores and concentrates are Chapter 26, not 81.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on tungsten from China?
faqs.answer: Unwrought tungsten and wrought tungsten from China pay the base rate + 25% Section 301 (note 31(j), heading 9903.91.11, since January 1, 2025) + 12.5% (the 2026 action): 44.1% for unwrought tungsten (8101.94). Tungsten powder pays 7% + 25% (note 31(b), since September 27, 2024) = 32%; tungsten wire 41.9%; scrap only its 2.8% base rate. Tungsten shot from China also carries antidumping (201.32% China-wide) and countervailing duty orders.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for tungsten carbide?
faqs.answer: It depends on the form. Tungsten carbide powder is a chemical, 2849.90.30 (5.5%). Cemented (sintered) carbide is a cermet: rods, blanks, wear parts and scrap generally fall in 8113.00.00 (3.7%), while plates, tips and inserts for tools, unmounted, are 8209.00.00 (4.6%). Cermets of 8113 pay the 2026 Section 301 duty and, from Canada, the 50% Section 338 duty.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on titanium?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on titanium
faqs.answer: Yes, a base rate: 15% on titanium sponge, ingot, powder and mill products (bars, plate, sheet, tube), 5.5% on titanium castings and articles, Free on scrap. All titanium lines are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duties, and no Section 232 tariff applies (a 2019 Section 232 finding on titanium sponge led to a working group, not tariffs). China pays 25% more (40% on sponge), Russia 70% on sponge and scrap. FTA partners (Korea, Israel, Chile, Australia) and USMCA goods pay nothing; civil aircraft tubes with attached fittings are Free.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for titanium sponge, sheet, scrap and powder?
faqs.answer: Unwrought titanium is 8108.20.00: sponge .10, powders .15, ingots .30, other .95 (15%). Scrap is 8108.30.00 (Free). Castings are 8108.90.30.30 and other titanium articles 8108.90.30.60 (5.5%). Mill products are 8108.90.60 (15%): blooms, sheet bars and slabs .20, bars, rods, profiles and wire .31, plates, sheets, strip and foil .45, tubes and pipes .60. Titanium dioxide is 2823.00.00 (Chapter 28), not Chapter 81.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on magnesium, and what is its tariff code?
faqs.answer: Unwrought magnesium of at least 99.8% is 8104.11.00 (8%), other unwrought magnesium (alloys) 8104.19.00 (6.5%), scrap 8104.20.00 (Free), raspings, granules and powder 8104.30.00 (4.4%), other articles 8104.90.00 (14.8¢/kg on magnesium content + 3.5%). All are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty. Chinese pure, granular and alloy magnesium also carry antidumping duty orders (the alloy order is in a sunset review begun October 1, 2026). Magnesium oxide, sulfate and other compounds are in Chapters 25 and 28.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on gallium, germanium and antimony?
faqs.answer: Unwrought gallium (8112.92.10) is 3%, unwrought germanium (8112.92.60) 2.6%, other germanium (8112.99.10) 4.4%, and antimony (8110) Free. All are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty. From China, gallium pays 25% more (28%) and wrought germanium 29.4%, while unwrought germanium and antimony pay no Section 301 duty. China's export controls on such minerals are Chinese rules, not U.S. duties; in November 2025 China committed to postpone and effectively eliminate its controls on rare earths and other critical minerals (Executive Order 14358).

faqs.question: What is the tariff on cobalt?
faqs.answer: Unwrought cobalt (other than alloys), mattes, powders and scrap are Free; cobalt alloys 4.4% and other cobalt articles 3.7% (8105). All cobalt lines are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty. Chinese cobalt pays 25% (List 3). USMCA, FTA and AGOA claims remove the base rate (Madagascar's cobalt enters Free). Cobalt ores are Chapter 26 and cobalt oxides Chapter 28.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on molybdenum, manganese and bismuth?
faqs.answer: Molybdenum powder pays 9.1¢/kg on molybdenum content + 1.2%, unwrought molybdenum 13.9¢/kg on molybdenum content + 1.9%, bars and other articles up to 6.6%; no molybdenum line is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty, so most suppliers add 10% or 12.5%. Unwrought manganese is 14% and exempt; manganese scrap (Free) and articles (3.7%) are not. Bismuth is Free and exempt; Chinese bismuth pays 25%.

faqs.question: What tariffs apply to critical minerals from Canada?
faqs.answer: USMCA-qualifying Canadian Chapter 81 metals (cobalt, tungsten, titanium and the rest) enter Free: USMCA removes the base rate and the 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.93). The exception is cermets (8113), which pay the 50% Section 338 duty (9903.03.14) since August 22, 2026, with or without USMCA. Without a USMCA claim, the 32 lines outside note 52(b) pay 10% more. The 2025 IEEPA duties on Canada ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What are cermets, and what is their HS code?
faqs.answer: Cermets are sintered composites of a ceramic and a metal, such as cemented carbides. Cermets and articles of cermets, including waste and scrap, are 8113.00.00 (3.7%); cermet plates, tips and inserts for tools, unmounted, are 8209.00.00 (4.6%), and inserts mounted on tools are classified with the tool. 8113 pays the 2026 Section 301 duty, 25% more from China (41.2% in total) and 50% more from Canada under Section 338.

faqs.question: What does HTS Chapter 81 cover?
faqs.answer: Chapter 81, "Other base metals; cermets; articles thereof", covers tungsten (8101), molybdenum (8102), tantalum (8103), magnesium (8104), cobalt (8105), bismuth (8106), titanium (8108), zirconium (8109), antimony (8110), manganese (8111), beryllium, chromium, hafnium, rhenium, thallium, cadmium, gallium, germanium, indium, niobium and vanadium (8112), and cermets (8113): 84 tariff lines from Free to 15%. Ores are in Chapter 26 and compounds in Chapter 28.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import these metals from?
searchedAs: where does the us get titanium
where does the us get most of its tungsten
where does the us get cobalt
does the us buy titanium from russia
faqs.answer: In 2025 the United States imported $3.92B of Chapter 81 metals and cermets. The largest suppliers were Japan ($567M), China ($475M), Germany ($411M), United Kingdom ($313M), Canada ($296M). The biggest product groups were titanium (8108, $1.19B), minor metals (8112, $649M), cobalt (8105, $486M). Imports from China fell from $746M in 2024 to $475M. Russia shipped $24M of titanium, which pays 70% (sponge and scrap) or column 2 rates.
